cim: Can the United States and China Cooperate to Control Artificial Intelligence?
kihagyva: P3: 46 pont, tendencia 20%, jóváhagyás után fordul
cim_eredeti: Can the United States and China Cooperate to Control Artificial Intelligence?
szoveg_eredeti:
Science and engineering bring to the world a new technology with military applications. The resulting weapons put immense power in the hands of those who control them, creating the threat of unprecedented destruction. The new weapons belong almost exclusively to two large countries that are engaged in bitter rivalry of global scope with each other. The two invest heavily in improving these weapons and expanding their supplies of them, leading to an arms race between them. The danger that the new weapons pose ultimately leads to limited cooperation between the two rivals, in the midst of their ongoing conflict, in the form of negotiated agreements placing limits on the new instruments of warfare.

This sequence of events describes the history of nuclear weapons from their creation and use during World War II to the arms control accords between the United States and the Soviet Union in the 1970s. Might the latest new military-related technology, Artificial Intelligence (AI), follow the same pattern? Might the United States and the People’s Republic of China find common ground in controlling this new technology, which they dominate? However desirable such an outcome may be, it is unlikely to be realized because of several fundamental differences between the two types of military instruments.

When serious arms control began a half century ago, nuclear weapons had become a mature technology. The basic innovations on which they were based – fission and fusion explosives and ballistic missiles capable of hurling them across oceans and continents in minutes – had already been made. The two rival superpowers had incorporated these innovations into their military forces and had found ways to live with the weapons making use of them without going to war. In fact, the arms control agreements of the 1970s can be seen in retrospect to have had the effect of ratifying an already stable military status quo between them. Washington and Moscow could have confidence that neither side’s ongoing programs of research and development in nuclear technology would confer a major advantage on the other, with one exception: if either side perfected a means of defending its territory against a large-scale ballistic missile attack, that would give it military superiority over iuts rival. The fear of such a development, as well as the common desire to avoid an expensive and possibly fruitless effort to build and deploy defenses, led the two countries to agree, in 1972, to place strict limits on the deployment of defensive systems.

In 2026 the technical possibilities of AI, by contrast, cannot be accurately foreseen but are surely very far from being exhausted. The uncertainty surrounding AI will make the American and Chinese governments less inclined to impose limits on it than were the American and Soviet governments for nuclear weapons fifty years ago. Other differences between the two technologies also make AI arms control unlikely.

Whereas the American and Soviet governments created and controlled nuclear weapons and the technologies that made them possible from the outset, American AI comes from the private sector. (This is also the case, up to a point, for China, but the Chinese government exercises far greater control over all aspects of the country that it governs than does its American counterpart.) Private companies own AI. The American federal government has road leeway, including over the private sector, in matters of national security but cannot arbitrarily take control of it for the purpose of carrying out an agreement with another country.

Relatedly, the physical processes at the heart of nuclear weaponry – nuclear fission and fusion – had at the beginning no applications beyond military ones; and in the eight decades since then only modest civilian uses have been found for them. The opposite is the case for AI, which already has an important role in the economy and, in the future, potentially a transformative one. Limiting it could therefore impose very high costs not only on its proprietors but on the whole of society, the possibility of which will act as a powerful disincentive to the imposition of such controls as part of twenty-first-century Sino-American arms control.

In the unlikely event that the United States and the People’s Republic could agree on the terms of a treaty placing limits on AI, they would also have to devise a method for ensuring that each was observing those terms. Verification became a central issue in the Soviet-American arms control negotiations because the Americans feared that the Soviet Union, would cheat on any agreement that it signed and, because it was a tightly closed society, the American government would not be able to detect the cheating. In the worst case, this risked giving the Soviet side a military advantage.

A technological advance made nuclear arms control possible. Earth-orbiting satellites launched in the 1960s could take photographs of the territory of each superpower. The Americans could thereby count the number of ballistic missiles and manned aircraft of intercontinental range the Soviets were deploying and thus could know whether or not the communist country had exceeded the agreed-upon limits. This meant, however, that arms control agreements could include only what could be reliably from tracked from space, which limited the scope of the initial arms control accords to very large objects.

Since AI consists of vast digital networks and complicated algorithms impenetrable to all but the most sophisticated scientists and engineers, it his hard to know what a verification regime for it would look like, let alone how it would be implemented. Yet such a regime would be necessary. The United States would not (and should not) simply take the word of the communist dictatorship in Beijing that was dong what it had said it would do: the people of Hong Kong can tell them something about the Communist Party of China’s record in keeping its promises.

Finally, bilateral Sino-American arms control would not eliminate the potential danger that AI poses because, although the two countries do dominate the cutting-edge development of the technology, they cannot keep less advanced but still potent versions out of the hands of others. Here AI reproduces another feature of the history of nuclear weapons – the problem of nuclear proliferation. The United States and the Soviet Union cooperated to address this problem with the Nonproliferation Treaty (NPT) of 1968, under the terms of which most countries pledged not to acquire these armaments. The counter-proliferation effort proved remarkably successful. Nuclear weapons have spread only very slowly, but for two reasons distinct from the NPT.

First, nuclear weapons are not easy to build. In particular, the fuel necessary for detonating a nuclear explosion is difficult to obtain or make. Second, the United States offered nuclear protection to many countries that could have obtained their own nuclear weapons, obviating, in their judgement, the need to do so.

Neither condition applies to AI, so the prospects for an equivalent to the NPT are poor. Open-weight AI models, mainly from China, are spreading rapidly; and neither the United States nor the People’s Republic can offer the kind of protection against AI-produced mischief that restricted the diffusion of nuclear weapons – not least because it is not fully clear at present what such protection would involve.

If AI arms control seems infeasible, however, it may also be unnecessary, or at least its absence may not have major adverse consequences. While the effort to increase the destructive firepower of weaponry is as old as war itself, the advent of munitions deriving their power from unlocking the energy at the heart of matter represented a massive increase in destructive potential, one without any real historical precedent. A single nuclear explosive can destroy an entire city, something not only impossible but inconceivable
